nodes.name: Conformally compact Riemannian manifold
nodes.statement: We call $(M,g)$ a \emph{conformally compact Riemannian manifold} if $M$ is the interior of a compact manifold $\overline M$ with boundary $\partial\overline M=X$ and there exists a smooth function $\rho:\overline{M}\to{\mathbb R}_{\geq 0}$ and a Riemannian metric $\gamma_{(0)}$ on $X$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $\rho|_{X}=0$; \item $d\rho\neq0$ at all points of $X$; \item $\rho^2 g$ can be extended continuously to $X$; \item $\rho^2 g|_{TX}=\gamma_{(0)}$. \end{itemize}
differentia: $M$ is the interior of a compact manifold $\overline M$ with boundary $\partial\overline M=X$
$\rho^2 g$ can be extended continuously to $X$
nodes.statement_short: (M,g) is conformally compact if a boundary defining function rho makes rho^2 g extend to the boundary, inducing gamma_(0).
also_stated_at: A ``conformally compact metric'' is a complete metric on the interior $M$ of a compact manifold with boundary $\overline{M}$, which can be conformally extended to the whole of $\overline{M}$ (see below for a more precise definition).

nodes.name: Hyperbolic space H^4 as conformally compact
nodes.statement: A good example to have in mind is the hyperbolic space $\mathbb {H}^4$ consisting of the upper-half of ${\mathbb R}^4$ with metric \begin{eqnarray} g=\frac{dx^2+dy^2+dz^2+dt^2}{t^2}, \end{eqnarray} and $\rho=t$.

nodes.name: Non-uniqueness of the defining function
nodes.statement: It is important to note that the defining function $\rho$ is non-unique: for any positive function $\lambda$ on $\overline{M}$, we may consider $\tilde\rho=\lambda\rho$ which has the same properties above with $\gamma_{(0)}$ replaced by $\tilde\gamma_{(0)}=\lambda^2\gamma_{(0)}$. Therefore a conformally compact metric on $M$ only defines a conformal structure on the boundary $X=\partial \overline{M}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaling rho by a positive function rescales gamma_(0) conformally, so only a boundary conformal structure is defined.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement: A hyperbolic metric is by definition a metric having a constant sectional curvature $-1/l^2$, where $l$ has units of length.

nodes.name: Asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement: A conformally compact metric $g$ is called \emph{asymptotically hyperbolic} if its sectional curvature is asymptotically $-1/l^2$.
also_stated_at: An important subclass of conformally compact metrics are the so-called ``asymptotically hyperbolic metrics''.

nodes.name: H^4 is asymptotically hyperbolic
nodes.statement: Obviously, $\mathbb {H}^4$ being conformally compact and hyperbolic is in particular asymptotically hyperbolic.

nodes.name: Asymptotically hyperbolic condition |d rho|^2 = rho^2/l^2
conclusions: The asymptotically hyperbolic condition is equivalent to $|d\rho|^2_{g}=\rho^2/l^2$ at $X$
nodes.statement_short: AH is equivalent to |d rho|_g^2 = rho^2/l^2 on X, read off from the leading Riemann tensor asymptotics.

nodes.name: Poincare-Einstein metric
nodes.statement: We also see from this formula that conformally compact Einstein metrics, i.e.\ ones satisfying the Riemannian version of Einstein equations, are automatically asymptotically hyperbolic; they are called \emph{Poincar\'e--Einstein metrics}.
differentia: satisfying the Riemannian version of Einstein equations
also_stated_at: Special examples of such asymptotically hyperbolic metrics are the conformally compact metrics satisfying the Einstein condition, known in the mathematical literature as Poincar\'e--Einstein metrics.

nodes.name: Boundary expansion of a conformally compact metric
nodes.statement: Near the boundary $X$, we can write any conformally compact metric as \begin{eqnarray} g=\frac{l^2}{ \rho^2}\Big(\alpha d\rho^2+d\rho\otimes\beta+\beta\otimes d\rho+\gamma\Big), \end{eqnarray} where $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are 1-parameter families of functions, 1-forms and symmetric $(2,0)$-tensors on $X$, with the following power series expansion \[ \alpha=1+\rho\alpha_{(1)}+\cdots,\qquad\beta=\beta_{(0)}+\rho\beta_{(1)}+\cdots,\qquad \gamma=\gamma_{(0)}+\rho\gamma_{(1)}+\cdots. \]

nodes.name: AH condition alpha=1
nodes.statement: The asymptotically hyperbolic condition is $\alpha=1$.

nodes.name: Fefferman-Graham normal form of an AH metric
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we can always achieve $\beta=0$ by an appropriate diffeomorphism: the gradient flow of $\rho$ with respect to $\rho^2 g$ identifies the level sets of $\rho$ and removes this mixed term. In the asymptotically hyperbolic setting, we can thus write the metric in the form: \begin{eqnarray} g=\frac{l^2}{\rho^2}d\rho^2+\frac{l^2}{\rho^2}\gamma \qquad \gamma=\gamma_{(0)}+\rho\gamma_{(1)}+\cdots. \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: In the  asymptotically hyperbolic setting
conclusions: we can always achieve $\beta=0$ by an appropriate diffeomorphism
nodes.statement_short: By a diffeomorphism (gradient flow of rho) the mixed term vanishes, giving the normal form g = l^2(d rho^2 + gamma)/rho^2.

nodes.name: Residual diffeomorphism freedom
nodes.statement: There still remains some diffeomorphism freedom: infinitesimal diffeomorphisms generated by vector fields $\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho\in\Gamma(T\overline{M})$ where the function $\lambda$ is $\rho$-independent and the vector field $\xi$ satisfies a certain condition. We thus have, essentially, a residual boundary diffeomorphism as well as freedom of local rescalings of the radial coordinate. The latter is equivalent to the freedom of conformal rescalings of the boundary metric.

nodes.name: Fefferman-Graham expansion (order-by-order solution)
nodes.statement: Now, it is an exercise to write down Einstein's equations for (\ref{FG}) and solve them order by order in terms of an initially given value of $\gamma_{(0)}$. The first two terms are given by \begin{eqnarray} \gamma_{(1)}=0,\qquad \gamma_{(2)}{}_{ab}=-R_{(0)}{}_{ab}+\frac{1}{4}R_{(0)}\gamma_{(0)}{}_{ab} \end{eqnarray} and the third remains undetermined but constrained to satisfy $$\gamma_{(0)}^{ab}\gamma_{(3)}{}_{ab}=0,\qquad \nabla_{(0)}{}^a\gamma_{(3)}{}_{ab}=0.$$ The remaining, higher-order terms, are then recursively determined algebraically from the previous terms.

conclusions: The first two terms are given by

The remaining, higher-order terms, are then recursively determined algebraically from the previous terms.
nodes.statement_short: Solving Einstein's equations order by order in FG gauge fixes gamma_(1), gamma_(2); gamma_(3) is trace- and divergence-free but free; higher orders are determined.

nodes.name: Obstruction (Fefferman-Graham)
nodes.statement: The unconstrained part of $\gamma_{(3)ab}$ is referred to as the {\it obstruction} by Fefferman-Graham.

nodes.name: Fefferman-Graham expansion
nodes.statement: We can interpret the expansion (\ref{FG}) as an instance of the initial value problem. Given the initial data on the boundary in the form of the boundary metric $\gamma_{(0)}$, as well as the constrained $\gamma_{(3)}$, which is best thought of as an initial momentum, we can propagate these data into the bulk, obtaining a Poincar\'e--Einstein metric, at least formally in a neighbourhood of the boundary. This is known as the \emph{Fefferman--Graham expansion}.
nodes.statement_short: The FG expansion propagates boundary data gamma_(0) and constrained gamma_(3) into a formal Poincare-Einstein metric near the boundary.

nodes.name: Expansion of the boundary volume density
nodes.statement: Using the tracelessness of $\gamma_{(3)}$, an easy calculation gives \begin{eqnarray}\nonumber \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma)} = \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1+\frac{1}{2} \rho^2 {\rm Tr}(\gamma_{(0)}^{-1} \gamma_{(2)})+ O(\rho^4) \right) = \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1-\frac{1}{8} \rho^2 R_{(0)}+ O(\rho^4)\right), \end{eqnarray} where we have used (\ref{gamma-2}) to get the second equality.
nodes.statement_short: sqrt(det gamma) = sqrt(det gamma_(0))(1 - rho^2 R_(0)/8 + O(rho^4)).

nodes.name: Cut-off volume V_epsilon
nodes.statement: The volume of the metric (\ref{FG}), up to a surface $\rho=\epsilon$ is then \begin{eqnarray} V_\epsilon = l^4 \int_\epsilon \frac{d\rho}{\rho^4} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} \left( 1-\frac{1}{8} \rho^2 R_{(0)}+ O(\rho^4)\right), \end{eqnarray} where ${X_\epsilon}$ is the surface $\rho=\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Renormalised volume (metric setting)
nodes.statement: Thus, the volume is given by \begin{eqnarray}\nonumber V_\epsilon = \frac{l^4 }{3\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} - \frac{l^4 }{8\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} R_{(0)} + {\rm finite\,\,\, terms}, \end{eqnarray} and the renormalised volume is then defined as \begin{eqnarray} RV:=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \left( V_\epsilon -\frac{l^4}{3\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} + \frac{l^4}{8\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} \sqrt{{\rm det}(\gamma_{(0)})} R_{(0)} \right). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: RV is the epsilon->0 limit of V_epsilon minus its 1/epsilon^3 and 1/epsilon divergences.

nodes.name: Renormalised volume is conformally invariant
nodes.statement: We note that the renormalized volume is independent of the choice of representative $\gamma_{(0)}$ of the conformal class on $X$.
conclusions: the renormalized volume is independent of the choice of representative $\gamma_{(0)}$ of the conformal class on $X$
also_stated_at: In even dimensions, and in particular in the case of 4D of interest for us here, the renormalised volume of a Poincar\'e--Einstein manifold is independent of the choice of $\rho$ and is thus an invariant of the metric in question.

nodes.name: Proof of conformal invariance of renormalised volume
nodes.statement: In fact for another representative $\tilde \gamma_{(0)}=\lambda^{2}\gamma_{(0)}$, the corresponding defining function is $\tilde \rho=\lambda\rho$ for an appropriate extension of $\lambda$ from the boundary into the bulk, and $\tilde{\epsilon}=\lambda^2 \epsilon$. Then the formula (\ref{RV}) takes exactly the same form in terms of the tilded quantities, which shows that it does not matter which representative in the conformal class of the boundary is used to compute it.
nodes.statement_short: Change representative gamma_(0) -> lambda^2 gamma_(0) with rho -> lambda rho; formula (RV) keeps the same form.

nodes.name: SO(3)-connection and its curvature
nodes.statement: Let $A^i$ be an ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection on a 4-manifold $M$, and $F^i = dA^i + (1/2) \epsilon^{ijk} A^j\wedge A^k$ be its curvature 2-forms.

nodes.name: Auxiliary matrix M
nodes.statement: Let $M^{ij}$ be a symmetric $3\times 3$ matrix of auxiliary fields.

nodes.name: Compactness of the manifold (temporary)
nodes.statement: Let us assume for the moment that the manifold in question is compact.

nodes.name: Connection action functional
nodes.statement: Consider the following action: \begin{eqnarray} S[A,M] = \int_M {\rm Tr}( M F\wedge F). \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Hypersurface constraint on M
nodes.statement: We also impose a constraint on the matrix $M$, that it lie on a co-dimension one hypersurface with defining equation \begin{eqnarray} g(M)=0 \end{eqnarray} in the space of symmetric $3\times 3$ matrices, determined by a real valued function $g$.

nodes.name: Einstein hypersurface
nodes.statement: Different hypersurfaces give different field equations; the hypersurface relevant to Einstein connections/metrics is given by \begin{eqnarray} g_{\rm E}(M) = {\rm Tr}(M^{-1}) - \Lambda, \end{eqnarray} where $4\Lambda$ is the scalar curvature.

nodes.name: Critical points give Einstein metrics
nodes.statement: The claim is that the critical points of (\ref{action}), with $M$ restricted to lie on (\ref{surface}) with $g$ given by (\ref{g-EH}) give rise to Einstein metrics.
assumptions: $M$ restricted to lie on (\ref{surface}) with $g$ given by (\ref{g-EH})
conclusions: the critical points of (\ref{action}), with $M$ restricted to lie on (\ref{surface}) with $g$ given by (\ref{g-EH}) give rise to Einstein metrics
also_stated_at: When the connection satisfies the Euler-Lagrange equations (\ref{eq-A}), (\ref{eq-M-gr}), the corresponding metric will be Einstein (see \cite{Herfray:2015fpa} for the proof).

nodes.name: Connection field equation
nodes.statement: Varying the action (\ref{action}) with respect to the connection we get \begin{eqnarray} d_A \left( M^{ij} F^j \right) =0. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Auxiliary volume form
nodes.statement: To do this, we introduce an auxiliary volume form ${\mathcal V}$.

nodes.name: Matrix X of curvature wedge products
nodes.statement: We can then write \begin{eqnarray} F^i\wedge F^j = X^{ij} \,{\mathcal V}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: X is defined only up to scale
nodes.statement: Note that a different choice of $\mathcal V$ changes the matrix $X^{ij}$ by multiplication by a function. The matrix $X$ is thus defined intrinsically only up to scale.

nodes.name: Action with Lagrange multiplier
nodes.statement: We can now write the action as \begin{eqnarray} S[A,M,\mu] = \int_M \left( {\rm Tr}(M X) - \mu \, g(M) \right) {\mathcal V}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Euler-Lagrange equation for M
nodes.statement: The Euler-Lagrange equations for $M$ are then \begin{eqnarray} X = \mu \frac{\partial g}{\partial M}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Derivative matrix dg/dM
nodes.statement: (Here, we write $\partial g/\partial M$ for the matrix defined by \[ \frac{\partial g}{\partial M^{ij}} A^{ji} = dg\Big|_{M}(A) \] for all symmetric $A^{ij}$.)

nodes.name: Pure connection formulation via Legendre transform
nodes.statement: Equation (\ref{eq-M}) can be solved, together with $g(M)=0$, for $M(X)$. This can then be substituted to (\ref{eq-A}) to obtain the ``pure connection'' formulation of field equations, in which we obtain second-order PDE's for the connection. Alternatively, one can insert the solution $M(X)$ back into the Lagrangian to obtain the ``pure connection'' action principle. One can check that the Lagrangian arising this way is just the Legendre transform of the function $g(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Solving (eq-M) for M(X) gives the pure connection formulation; its Lagrangian is the Legendre transform of g.

nodes.name: Strategy: first-order PDE for M
nodes.statement: However, in many circumstances a more useful approach is not to solve for $M(X)$, but to interpret (\ref{eq-A}) as a first-order PDE on the matrix $M$. Solving it one can then find $X$ from (\ref{eq-M}) and thus obtain a set of first-order PDE's on the connection components. It is this strategy that will be followed below for the asymptotically hyperbolic connections.

nodes.name: Derivation of the Einstein-case relation
nodes.statement: Let us illustrate all this for the Einstein case (\ref{g-EH}). In this case we can rewrite (\ref{eq-M}) as $M X = - \mu M^{-1}$. Taking the trace and using the condition $g_E(M)=0$ we obtain $\mu$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite (eq-M) as MX = -mu M^{-1}, take the trace and use g_E(M)=0 to find mu.

nodes.name: X in terms of M for the Einstein case
nodes.statement: Thus, all in all for the Einstein case \begin{eqnarray} X = \frac{1}{\Lambda} {\rm Tr}(M X) M^{-2}, \end{eqnarray} which gives $X$ in terms of $M$, up to scale.

nodes.name: Conformal metric of a connection
nodes.statement: First, one constructs the conformal metric. This is the unique conformal structure that makes the triple of curvature 2-forms $F^i$ self-dual. Explicitly, \begin{eqnarray} \sqrt{{\rm det(g)}} \, g_{\mu\nu} \sim \tilde{\epsilon}^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} \epsilon^{ijk} F^i_{\mu\alpha} F^j_{\nu\beta} F^k_{\gamma\delta}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The conformal structure is the unique one making the curvature 2-forms F^i self-dual (Urbantke formula).

nodes.name: Volume form of the connection metric
nodes.statement: Second, one fixes the volume form ${\mathcal V}_g$ of the metric to be \begin{eqnarray} - 2\Lambda \, {\mathcal V}_g = {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F). \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Action as total volume
nodes.statement: With this choice of volume form, the action (\ref{action}) has the geometric interpretation of the total volume, up to overall scale. The numerical factor in this formula is adjusted to agree with some conventions introduced later.

nodes.name: Deformed Einstein connections
nodes.statement: An interesting class of deformations of the Einstein condition is obtained by simply changing the codimension-one hypersurface that the matrix $M$ is constrained to lie on, in the action (\ref{action}). This corresponds to changing the function $g$ in the equation $g(M)=0$.

nodes.name: g_inst gives self-dual GR
nodes.statement: Repacing $M$ by $M^{-1}$ in this function, setting $g_{inst}={\rm Tr}(M) - \Lambda$, turns out to give self-dual General Relativity, with solutions being half-flat Einstein metrics, see \cite{Herfray:2015fpa} for a discussion of this.
assumptions: setting $g_{inst}={\rm Tr}(M) - \Lambda$
conclusions: turns out to give self-dual General Relativity, with solutions being half-flat Einstein metrics

nodes.name: Modified theory g_mod = det M - Lambda
nodes.statement: Another very interesting modification that can be considered is to set \begin{eqnarray} g_{mod}(M) = {\rm det}(M) - \Lambda. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Results apply to all deformed theories
nodes.statement: Details of these modified theories will not be important for us here, because we will be solving the arising equations in general for an arbitrary function $g(M)$. All our results below apply equally to the modified theories as well as to GR.

nodes.name: Metric of a deformed theory
nodes.statement: In the deformed case, one continues to define the metric by the condition that the curvature 2-forms are self-dual. The volume form is then fixed to be a constant multiple of the form ${\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F)$, so that the action (\ref{action}) continues to receive the interpretation of the total volume of the space.

nodes.name: Adapted coframe
nodes.statement: First we choose a local coframe for $g$ adapted to the chosen conformal compactification $$\theta^i=\frac{l}{\rho}e^i,\qquad\theta^4=\frac{l}{\rho}d\rho,$$ where $e^i$ denotes a 1-parameter family of local coframes for the 1-parameter family of metrics $\gamma$ on $X$.
nodes.section: 4.1 ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric

nodes.name: Computation of the spin connection
nodes.statement: The spin connection is then computed by decomposing the structure equation as $$\begin{cases}d\theta^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge \theta^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge \theta^4=0 \cr d\theta^4+\omega^4{}_i\wedge \theta^i=0, \end{cases}$$ or, equivalently $$\begin{cases} de^i-\frac{1}{\rho}d\rho\wedge e^i+\omega^i{}_j\wedge e^j+\omega^i{}_4\wedge d\rho=0 \cr \omega^4{}_i\wedge e^i=0.\end{cases}$$ These equations can be readily solved in terms of the (co-)triad $e^i$ and the associated $\gamma$-compatible spin connection ${}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j$ $$\begin{cases} \omega^i{}_j={}^\gamma\omega^i{}_j-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)-\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)d\rho \cr \omega^{4i}=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)+\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)e^j. \end{cases}$$ Here dot denotes the derivative with respect to $\rho$, and $\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)$ is the metric product of 1-forms $\dot e^i$ and $e^j$.
nodes.section: 4.1 ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement_short: Decompose Cartan's structure equations for the adapted coframe and solve for the spin connection.

nodes.name: Self-dual connection of an AH metric
nodes.statement: We may now express the $SU(2)$-connection $A^i$ in terms of the 1-parameter families of (co-)frames and spin connections on $X$ as \begin{eqnarray} A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+{}^\gamma\omega^i-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\gamma(\dot e^i,e^j)+\gamma(\dot e^j,e^i)\Big)e^j+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{ijk}\gamma(\dot e^j,e^k)d\rho, \end{eqnarray} where ${}^\gamma\omega^i=-(1/2)\epsilon^{ijk}\, {}^\gamma\omega^{jk}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric
nodes.statement_short: The self-dual Levi-Civita connection of an AH metric is e^i/rho + gamma-spin connection + dot-e terms + a d rho term.

nodes.name: Einstein AH metric: O(1) part of connection
nodes.statement: Let us note that for an asymptotically hyperbolic metric that is also Einstein, equation (\ref{gamma-2}) is satisfied. The first of these conditions then implies that the third term in (\ref{A-metric}) starts with a term $O(\rho)$, so that the connection ${}^\gamma\omega^i$ compatible with $e^i$ is the only contribution at order $O(1)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 ${\rm SO}(3)$-connection of an asymptotically hyperbolic metric

nodes.name: SU(2)-bundle P over the compactification
nodes.statement: Let $P\to\overline M$ be an ${\rm SO}(3)$ or ${\rm SU}(2)$-bundle over $\overline M$ and denote by $P|_M\to M$ its restriction to $M$ and by $P|_X\to X$ its restriction to $X$.

nodes.name: P|_X isomorphic to frame bundle
nodes.statement: We require $P|_X$ to be abstractly isomorphic to the frame bundle of $X$.

nodes.name: Asymptotically hyperbolic SU(2)-connection
nodes.statement: We shall call an ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection $A^i$ on $P|_M$ \emph{asymptotically hyperbolic} if there exists a smooth function $\rho:\overline{M}\to{\mathbb R}_+$ and a smooth connection $\omega$ on $P$ defined on the whole of $\overline{M}$, such that \begin{itemize} \item $\rho$ is a boundary defining function, i.e., $\rho|_{X}=0$ and $d\rho|_{X}\neq0$; \item The endomorphism-valued 1-form $\rho(A^i-\omega^i)$ extends smoothly to $X$; \item The restriction $\rho(A^i-\omega^i)|_{TX}=e^i_{(0)}$ is a coframing for $X$. Equivalently, $\rho(A-\omega)|_{TX} \in T^*X \otimes \mathfrak(P|_X)$ gives an isomorphism $TX \to \mathfrak{su}(P|_X)$. \end{itemize}
differentia: $\rho$ is a boundary defining function, i.e., $\rho|_{X}=0$ and $d\rho|_{X}\neq0$
The restriction $\rho(A^i-\omega^i)|_{TX}=e^i_{(0)}$ is a coframing for $X$
nodes.statement_short: A connection is AH if rho(A - omega) extends smoothly to the boundary and restricts there to a coframe of X.

nodes.name: Analogy with conformal compactness
nodes.statement: The last condition here should is the analogue of the condition that a conformally compact metric $g$ should have $\rho^2g|_X$ a metric on $X$.

nodes.name: AH definition independent of choices
nodes.statement: It is immediate that the definition does not depend on the choices of $\rho$ or $\omega$.
conclusions: the definition does not depend on the choices of $\rho$ or $\omega$

nodes.name: Boundary metric gamma_(0) of an AH connection
nodes.statement: Given an asymptotically hyperbolic connection, we can define a metric $\gamma_{(0)}$ on $X$ by declaring $e^i_{(0)}$to be an orthonormal coframe. This fixes an isomorphism $P|_X \to TX$.

nodes.name: Reference connection omega_(0)
nodes.statement: It is then convenient to take $\omega^i$ to be an arbitrary extension of the Levi-Civita connection $\omega_{(0)}^i$ of $\gamma_{(0)}$ on $P|_X$ to the whole of $P \to \overline{M}$.

nodes.name: General form of an AH connection
nodes.statement: Thus, in general, an asymptotically hyperbolic ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection may be written as: \begin{eqnarray} A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i_{(0)}+\omega^i_{(0)}+a^i+b^id\rho \end{eqnarray} where \[ a^i=a^i_{(0)}+\rho a^i_{(1)}+\cdots, \qquad b^i=b^i_{(0)}+\rho b^i_{(1)}+\cdots \] are 1-parameter families of 1-forms and functions on $X$, respectively.

nodes.name: Metric of an AH connection is AH
nodes.statement: In this subsection we compute the metric associated to an asymptotically hyperbolic connection. We find it to be asymptotically hyperbolic.
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
assumptions: the metric associated to an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
conclusions: We find it to be asymptotically hyperbolic.

nodes.name: Connection vs metric: first-order pole suffices
nodes.statement: As we have already emphasised in the Introduction, one of the main differences between the metric and connection setups is that in the later case the requirement (\ref{as-hyperb-conn}) of a first-order pole in the radial coordinate automatically gives rise to connections asymptotically satisfying the field equations. This should be contrasted to the metric case, where the requirement (\ref{FG}) of a second-order pole only gives the conformal compactness condition and an extra condition must be imposed to obtain asymptotically hyperbolic metrics.
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection

nodes.name: Computation of the metric of an AH connection
nodes.statement: The metric is computed in two steps. First, we need to find a metric that makes the curvature 2-forms self-dual. The curvature of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection is: \begin{eqnarray} F^i = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\Sigma^i_{(0)}+\mathcal{O} (1) = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\left( d\rho\wedge e^i_{(0)}-\frac{\epsilon^{ijk}}{2}e^j_{(0)}\wedge e^k_{(0)} \right )+\mathcal{O} (1). \end{eqnarray} Note that there is no $1/\rho$ term here because $d_{\omega_{(0)}} e_{(0)}^i = 0$ (since $\omega_{(0)}$ is the Levi-Civita connection of $\gamma_{(0)}$). The conformal metric in which these 2-forms are self-dual is a multiple of \[ \frac{1}{\rho^2}\left(d\rho^2+ \sum_{i} e^i_{(0)}\otimes e^i_{(0)}\right)+\mathcal{O} (1). \] As is clear from (\ref{curv-asympt}), asymptotically the matrix (\ref{X}) of wedge products $X^{ij}\sim\delta^{ij}$. From (\ref{eq-M-gr}) this implies that the matrix $M$ is asymptotically pure trace $M^{ij}\sim \delta^{ij}$. This in particular implies that the field equation (\ref{eq-A}) is automatically satisfied, as it reduces to the Bianchi identity for the curvature. Thus, asymptotically hyperbolic connections are automatically asymptotic solutions of the field equations. To fix the metric, we compute, asymptotically \begin{eqnarray} {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) = \frac{3}{\Lambda}{\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = - \frac{3}{\Lambda} \frac{6}{\rho^4} d\rho\wedge e_{(0)}^1\wedge e_{(0)}^2\wedge e_{(0)}^3. \end{eqnarray} From (\ref{volume}), remembering $\Lambda=-3/l^2$, we immediately get that the metric defined by the connection, asymptotically, is \begin{eqnarray} \frac{l^2}{\rho^2}\left(d\rho^2+ \sum_{i} e^i_{(0)}\otimes e^i_{(0)}\right)+\mathcal{O} (1), \end{eqnarray} which is an asymptotically hyperbolic metric of sectional curvature $-1/l^2$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement_short: Compute the leading curvature, its self-dual conformal metric, then fix the volume via Tr(MF^F). Leading X ~ delta forces M ~ delta so (eq-A) reduces to Bianchi.

nodes.name: AH connections are asymptotic solutions
nodes.statement: Thus, asymptotically hyperbolic connections are automatically asymptotic solutions of the field equations.
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
conclusions: asymptotically hyperbolic connections are automatically asymptotic solutions of the field equations

nodes.name: Asymptotic curvature
nodes.statement: The metric is computed in two steps. First, we need to find a metric that makes the curvature 2-forms self-dual. The curvature of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection is: \begin{eqnarray} F^i = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\Sigma^i_{(0)}+\mathcal{O} (1) = -\frac{1}{\rho^2}\left( d\rho\wedge e^i_{(0)}-\frac{\epsilon^{ijk}}{2}e^j_{(0)}\wedge e^k_{(0)} \right )+\mathcal{O} (1). \end{eqnarray} Note that there is no $1/\rho$ term here because $d_{\omega_{(0)}} e_{(0)}^i = 0$ (since $\omega_{(0)}$ is the Levi-Civita connection of $\gamma_{(0)}$).
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement_short: Compute the leading 1/rho^2 curvature of an AH connection.

nodes.name: Self-dual conformal metric
nodes.statement: The conformal metric in which these 2-forms are self-dual is a multiple of \[ \frac{1}{\rho^2}\left(d\rho^2+ \sum_{i} e^i_{(0)}\otimes e^i_{(0)}\right)+\mathcal{O} (1). \]
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement_short: Read off the conformal metric making the leading curvature self-dual.

nodes.name: Field equations hold asymptotically
nodes.statement: As is clear from (\ref{curv-asympt}), asymptotically the matrix (\ref{X}) of wedge products $X^{ij}\sim\delta^{ij}$. From (\ref{eq-M-gr}) this implies that the matrix $M$ is asymptotically pure trace $M^{ij}\sim \delta^{ij}$. This in particular implies that the field equation (\ref{eq-A}) is automatically satisfied, as it reduces to the Bianchi identity for the curvature. Thus, asymptotically hyperbolic connections are automatically asymptotic solutions of the field equations.
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement_short: X ~ delta gives M ~ delta, so (eq-A) reduces to the Bianchi identity.

nodes.name: Fix the volume form
nodes.statement: To fix the metric, we compute, asymptotically \begin{eqnarray} {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) = \frac{3}{\Lambda}{\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = - \frac{3}{\Lambda} \frac{6}{\rho^4} d\rho\wedge e_{(0)}^1\wedge e_{(0)}^2\wedge e_{(0)}^3. \end{eqnarray} From (\ref{volume}), remembering $\Lambda=-3/l^2$, we immediately get that the metric defined by the connection, asymptotically, is \begin{eqnarray} \frac{l^2}{\rho^2}\left(d\rho^2+ \sum_{i} e^i_{(0)}\otimes e^i_{(0)}\right)+\mathcal{O} (1), \end{eqnarray} which is an asymptotically hyperbolic metric of sectional curvature $-1/l^2$.
nodes.section: 4.3 Metric of an asymptotically hyperbolic connection
nodes.statement_short: Use the volume normalisation to get an AH metric of curvature -1/l^2.

nodes.name: Boundary term of the action variation
nodes.statement: The variation of ${\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F)$ produces a boundary term \begin{eqnarray} \delta \int {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) = 2 \int_X {\rm Tr}( M F \wedge \delta A) + \ldots, \end{eqnarray} where the dots stand for terms proportional to field equations.

nodes.name: Boundary condition: M asymptotically proportional to identity
nodes.statement: A convenient choice of boundary conditions for the variational principle is then as follows. Instead of fixing the connection on the boundary, which is inconvenient because the connection has a first order pole there, we can require that asymptotically and to a sufficiently high order in the radial coordinate expansion (see below) the matrix of auxiliary fields is a multiple of the identity matrix.

nodes.name: Chern-Simons boundary term cancels boundary variation
nodes.statement: Then the boundary term (\ref{b-term}) arising in the variation of the action is cancelled by the Chern--Simons invariant of the restriction of the connection to the boundary \begin{eqnarray} S^{CS}_X[A] = \int_X \left( A^i \wedge dA^i + \frac{1}{3} \epsilon^{ijk} A^i\wedge A^j\wedge A^k\right), \end{eqnarray} which has the property \begin{eqnarray} \delta S^{CS}_X[A] = 2 \int_X {\rm Tr}(F \wedge \delta A). \end{eqnarray} Thus, with the boundary condition being those on $M$, the required boundary term is just the Chern--Simons invariant of the boundary connection.
assumptions: with the boundary condition being those on $M$
conclusions: the required boundary term is just the Chern--Simons invariant of the boundary connection
nodes.statement_short: With M ~ identity at the boundary, the boundary variation is cancelled by the Chern-Simons functional of the boundary connection.

nodes.name: 3+1 decomposition of the connection
nodes.statement: We fix a boundary defining function $\rho\in C^\infty(M,{\mathbb R}_{\geq 0})$ and decompose the connection $A^i$ as $$A^i=\alpha^i+\beta^id\rho$$ where $\alpha^i$ and $\beta^i$ are 1-parameter families of 1-forms and functions on $X$.

nodes.name: Curvature in 3+1 split
nodes.statement: The curvature of $A$ is then $$F_A^i=f_\alpha^i-(\dot\alpha^i-d^X_\alpha\beta^i)\wedge d\rho,$$ where $d^X_\alpha$ is the covariant exterior derivative with respect to connection $\alpha^i$ along the hypersurface $\rho=\text{const}$, and $f^i_\alpha$ is the curvature of $\alpha^i$.
also_stated_at: As before, we decompose the connection $A^i$ as $$A^i=\alpha^i+\beta^id\rho,$$ and its curvature as $$F_A^i=f_\alpha^i-(\dot\alpha^i-d^X_\alpha\beta^i)\wedge d\rho,$$ where $d^X_\alpha$ is the covariant exterior derivative with respect to connection $\alpha^i$ along the hypersurface $\rho=\text{const}$, and $f^i_\alpha$ is the curvature of $\alpha^i$.

nodes.name: Wedge-product matrix in 3+1 form
nodes.statement: We may define the matrix $X^{ij}$ of curvature wedge products (up to scale) as \begin{eqnarray} X^{ij} \sim f_\alpha^{(i}\wedge (\dot\alpha^{j)}-d^X_\alpha\beta^{j)})\wedge d\rho. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: 3+1 decomposition of the field equations
nodes.statement: Defining the momentum $\pi^i$ canonically conjugate to $\alpha^i$ by \begin{eqnarray} \pi^i = M^{ij} f^j_\alpha, \end{eqnarray} the 3+1 decomposition of the field equation (\ref{eq-A}) reads \begin{eqnarray} \begin{cases} \dot\pi^i+[\beta,\pi]^i=d^X_\alpha\Big(M^{ij}(\dot\alpha^j-d^X_\alpha\beta^j)\Big), \cr d^X_\alpha \pi^i=0. \end{cases} \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: With momentum pi = M f_alpha, the field equation splits into evolution equations and the Gauss constraint d_alpha pi = 0.

nodes.name: Evolution and constraint equations
nodes.statement: The first set of equations can be viewed as evolution equations for the momentum 2-forms $\pi^i$. However, it is better to think of them as first-order evolution equations for the matrix $M^{ij}$. The matrix $M^{ij}$ then determines $X^{ij}$ via (\ref{eq-M}), which in turn determines the evolution of $\alpha^i$ via (\ref{X-alpha}). The second set of equations are the constraints that the matrix $M^{ij}$ should satisfy, relating $M^{ij}$ to $X^{ij}$. One of the important features of the connection formulation is that there are only 3 constraint equations to be satisfied, to be compared with 4 diffeomorphism constraints in the metric approach. We further discuss the evolution equations (\ref{feqs}) from the Hamiltonian viewpoint in the Appendix.
nodes.statement_short: Evolution equations are first-order for M; only 3 constraints versus 4 diffeomorphism constraints in the metric approach.

nodes.name: A is asymptotically hyperbolic
nodes.statement: Let us now assume $A^i$ to be an asymptotically hyperbolic connection.

nodes.name: Temporal gauge beta=0
nodes.statement: For now, we just fix a part of the gauge freedom, by setting $\beta^i=0$.

nodes.name: Temporal gauge is attainable
nodes.statement: This can always be done by e.g. an ${\rm SO}(3)$ gauge transformation.

nodes.name: Frame expansion e^i
nodes.statement: We then write the $\alpha^i$ part of the connection in the form $$\alpha^i=\frac{1}{\rho}e^i+\omega^i_{(0)},$$ with $$ e^i = e^i_{(0)} + \rho \, e^i_{(1)} + \ldots,$$ and $\omega_{(0)}$ being the Levi-Civita connection of the frame $e_{(0)}$.

nodes.name: Connection gauge differs from FG gauge
nodes.statement: Note that the gauge-fixing condition $\beta^i=0$ is not compatible with the gauge used in the metric setting, see (\ref{FG}). Indeed, as we have previously computed, the connection corresponding to metric (\ref{FG}) is of the form (\ref{A-metric}), and in particular has a $d\rho$ term. The gauge $\beta^i=0$, quite convenient in calculations, will thus fail to produce a metric in the gauge (\ref{FG}). This just means that the most natural coordinate systems used in the metric and connection settings are different.

nodes.name: Spatial curvature of alpha and boundary derivative D
nodes.statement: The spatial curvature of $\alpha$ is given by \begin{eqnarray} f_\alpha^i=\frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{ijk}e^j\wedge e^k+\frac{1}{\rho}D e^i+f^i_{(0)}, \end{eqnarray} where $D\equiv d^X_{\omega_{(0)}}$ is the covariant derivative along the boundary $X$ with respect to $\omega_{(0)}$ and $f^i_{(0)}: = d\omega_{(0)}^i + (1/2)\epsilon^{ijk} \omega_{(0)}^j\omega_{(0)}^k$ is the curvature of $\omega_{(0)}$.

nodes.name: Matrix X via volume form V_0
nodes.statement: We now define the matrix $X^{ij}$ via \begin{eqnarray} f_\alpha^{(i}\wedge \dot{\alpha}^{j)} = X^{ij}\, {\mathcal V}_0, \qquad {\mathcal V}_0 = \frac{1}{\rho^4} d\rho\wedge \frac{1}{6}\epsilon^{ijk} e^i_{(0)}\wedge e^j_{(0)}\wedge e^k_{(0)}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Expansion of X starts with the identity
nodes.statement: The reason for choosing this volume form to define $X^{ij}$ is that its expansion in powers of $\rho$ starts with the identity matrix \begin{eqnarray} X^{ij} = \delta^{ij} + \rho X^{ij}_{(1)} +\ldots. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: M is asymptotically a multiple of identity
nodes.statement: The fact that the expansion for $X^{ij}$ starts with the identity implies that also the matrix $M^{ij}$, which is algebraically expressed in terms of $X^{ij}$ via (\ref{eq-M}), to leading order is a multiple of the identity matrix.
assumptions: the expansion for $X^{ij}$ starts with the identity
conclusions: the matrix $M^{ij}$, which is algebraically expressed in terms of $X^{ij}$ via (\ref{eq-M}), to leading order is a multiple of the identity matrix

nodes.name: Einstein case series for M
nodes.statement: For example, for the Einstein case we have \begin{eqnarray} \frac{\Lambda}{3} M = \sum_n (-1)^n \left( \frac{3\Psi}{\Lambda}\right)^n, \end{eqnarray} where $\Psi$ is a trace free matrix whose expansion starts with order $\rho$ (or higher).

nodes.name: Normalised matrix m
nodes.statement: So, we write \begin{eqnarray} M \sim m^{ij} = \delta^{ij} + \rho m^{ij}_{(1)} + \ldots, \end{eqnarray} for an appropriate multiple of $M$.

nodes.name: Evolution equation for m
nodes.statement: We can now write down the first of the equations in (\ref{feqs}) as an equation on the matrix $m\sim M$, where for a general theory an appropriate multiple of $M$ is taken so that the expansion for $m$ starts with the identity matrix. After some cancelations and rewriting, the equation reads \begin{eqnarray} \dot{m}^{ij} \left( \frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{jkl}e^k\wedge e^l+\frac{1}{\rho}D e^j+f^j_{(0)}\right) = (Dm^{ij})\wedge \left( -\frac{1}{\rho^2} e^i + \frac{1}{\rho} \dot{e}^i\right) \\ \nonumber + \frac{1}{\rho} (\epsilon^{ikj} m^{jl} - m^{ij} \epsilon^{jkl}) e^k \wedge \left( -\frac{1}{\rho^2} e^l + \frac{1}{\rho} \dot{e}^l\right). \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Leading-order argument for m-exp
nodes.statement: The left-had-side starts with terms of the order $1/\rho^2$, while there is a term of order $1/\rho^3$ on the right. This term cancels only when the expansion of $m$ starts with a multiple of the identity matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Compare orders: the 1/rho^3 term on the right cancels only if m starts with a multiple of the identity.

nodes.name: m starts with the identity (from the evolution equation)
nodes.statement: So, this equation once again tells us (\ref{m-exp}) should hold.

nodes.name: m_(1) = 0
nodes.statement: We get an equation for $m_{(1)}$ by keeping terms of order $1/\rho^2$ on both sides. We get \begin{eqnarray} \dot{m}^{ij} \frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{jkl}e^k_{(0)}\wedge e^l_{(0)} + (\epsilon^{ikj} m^{jl}_{(1)} - m^{ij}_{(1)} \epsilon^{jkl}) e^k_{(0)} \wedge e^l_{(0)} =0. \end{eqnarray} We now use \begin{eqnarray} e^i\wedge e^j = \epsilon^{ijk} \frac{1}{2} \epsilon^{klm} e^l\wedge e^m \end{eqnarray} to get \begin{eqnarray} 0=m^{ij}_{(1)} + (\epsilon^{ikn} m^{nl}_{(1)} - m^{in}_{(1)} \epsilon^{nkl})\epsilon^{klj}= - 2m^{ij}_{(1)} + \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(m_{(1)}), \end{eqnarray} which implies that \begin{eqnarray} m_{(1)}=0. \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: keeping terms of order $1/\rho^2$ on both sides
nodes.statement_short: The order-1/rho^2 part of the evolution equation forces the first-order coefficient m_(1) to vanish.

nodes.name: m_(2) = 0
nodes.statement: We get $m_{(2)}$ by exactly the same logic, keeping terms of order $1/\rho$ on both sides. We get \begin{eqnarray} 0=2m^{ij}_{(2)} + (\epsilon^{ikn} m^{nl}_{(2)} - m^{in}_{(2)} \epsilon^{nkl})\epsilon^{klj}= - m^{ij}_{(2)} + \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(m_{(2)}), \end{eqnarray} which implies that \begin{eqnarray} m_{(2)}=0. \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: keeping terms of order $1/\rho$ on both sides

nodes.name: Only the trace of m_(3) is constrained (obstruction)
nodes.statement: The new phenomenon appears at the next order, where we keep $O(1)$ terms. We now get \begin{eqnarray} 0=3m^{ij}_{(3)} + (\epsilon^{ikn} m^{nl}_{(3)} - m^{in}_{(3)} \epsilon^{nkl})\epsilon^{klj}= \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(m_{(3)}). \end{eqnarray} So, in this case the evolution equation only constraints the trace part of $m_{(3)}$ to vanish. Its trace free part remains arbitrary.
assumptions: we keep $O(1)$ terms
conclusions: the evolution equation only constraints the trace part of $m_{(3)}$ to vanish
Its trace free part remains arbitrary.
nodes.statement_short: At O(1) the evolution equation only forces Tr m_(3)=0; the trace-free part of m_(3) is free (the analogue of the FG obstruction).

nodes.name: Constraint equation in the expansion
nodes.statement: The second constraint equation in (\ref{feqs}) takes the form \begin{eqnarray} D\left( m^{ij} \left( \frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{jkl}e^k\wedge e^l+\frac{1}{\rho}D e^j+f^j_{(0)} \right) \right) + \frac{1}{\rho} \epsilon^{ijk} e^j \wedge m^{kn} \left( \frac{1}{\rho}D e^n+f^n_{(0)}\right) =0. \end{eqnarray} We dropped one of the terms inside the second pair of brackets here, because it is easy to see that it is proportional to $\epsilon^{ijk} m^{jk}$, which is zero in view of the symmetry of $m$.

nodes.name: Transversality constraint on m_(3)
nodes.statement: As we already know from the considerations above, the expansion for $m$, after the leading identity matrix term, continues with a term of order $\rho^3$, which is trace free. Then the leading order term in (\ref{constraint}) is \begin{eqnarray} (Dm^{ij}_{(3)})\wedge \epsilon^{jkl} e^k_{(0)}\wedge e^l_{(0)}=0, \end{eqnarray} which gives a further restriction on the matrix $m$.
assumptions: the expansion for $m$, after the leading identity matrix term, continues with a term of order $\rho^3$, which is trace free
conclusions: (Dm^{ij}_{(3)})\wedge \epsilon^{jkl} e^k_{(0)}\wedge e^l_{(0)}=0,
nodes.statement_short: The leading constraint gives a divergence-type (transversality) condition on the trace-free m_(3).

nodes.name: Trace-free parts of X_(1), X_(2) vanish
nodes.statement: From the fact that the matrix $m\sim M$ has an expansion of the form $m = {\mathbb I} + \rho^3 m_{(3)}+\ldots$, together with the fact that $X$ is algebraically determined by $M$ up to scale, see (\ref{eq-M}), we can immediately deduce that in (\ref{X-exp}) \begin{eqnarray} X_{(1)}^{ij}\Big|_{tf}= X_{(2)}^{ij}\Big|_{tf}=0. \end{eqnarray} We can only conclude that the trace free parts vanish, because the trace part of $X$ is not constrained by the equation (\ref{eq-M}) (indeed $X$ only makes invariant sense up to overall scale).
assumptions: the matrix $m\sim M$ has an expansion of the form $m = {\mathbb I} + \rho^3 m_{(3)}+\ldots$
$X$ is algebraically determined by $M$ up to scale

nodes.name: Matrix gamma^{ij}
nodes.statement: To this end, it is convenient to write \begin{eqnarray} e^i = \gamma^{ij} e^j_{(0)}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Formula for X in terms of frames
nodes.statement: The matrix $X$ is given by \begin{eqnarray} X^{ij} \frac{1}{6}\epsilon^{ijk} e^i_{(0)}\wedge e^j_{(0)}\wedge e^k_{(0)} = \left( \frac{1}{2} \epsilon^{(i|kl} e^k\wedge e^l + \rho D e^{(i} + \rho^2 f^{(i}_{(0)}\right) \wedge \left( e^{j)} - \rho \dot{e}^{j)}\right). \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: X_(1) in terms of gamma_(1)
nodes.statement: A simple computation gives \begin{eqnarray} X^{ij}_{(1)} = \epsilon^{(i|kl} \gamma^{kn}_{(1)} \epsilon^{nl|j)} = \delta^{ij} {\rm Tr}(\gamma_{(1)}) - \gamma_{(1)}^{(ij)}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Only trace-free part of gamma_(1) determined
nodes.statement: It is clear that we can only conclude from (\ref{X-12}) that the trace free part of $\gamma_{(1)}$ vanishes. To determine all of it we need to do more gauge-fixing.

nodes.name: Complete gauge fixing
nodes.statement: We fix the gauge completely. Thus, we require that $\gamma$ be symmetric and, also, that all terms except $\gamma_{(0)}={\mathbb I}$ be trace free \begin{eqnarray} \gamma^{ij}=\gamma^{(ij)}, \qquad {\rm Tr}(\gamma_{(n)})=0, \quad n>1. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Admissibility of the gauge
nodes.statement: The fact that this gauge condition, together with the imposed earlier $\beta^i=0$ is an admissible gauge, is demonstrated in the Appendix.
conclusions: this gauge condition, together with the imposed earlier $\beta^i=0$ is an admissible gauge

nodes.name: gamma_(1) = 0
nodes.statement: Having fixed the gauge, the equation (\ref{X-12}) with (\ref{eq-gamma-1}) fix \begin{eqnarray} \gamma_{(1)}^{ij}=0. \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: Having fixed the gauge

nodes.name: X_(2) in terms of gamma_(2) and curvature
nodes.statement: Taking (\ref{gamma-1}) into account, it is easy to compute $X_{(2)}$. Taking into account the gauge-fixing conditions (\ref{gauge}) we get \begin{eqnarray} X_{(2)}^{ij} = - 2\gamma_{(2)}^{ij} + f^{ij}_{(0)}, \end{eqnarray} where we introduced the components of the curvature \begin{eqnarray} f^i_{(0)} = \frac{1}{2} f^{ij}_{(0)} \epsilon^{jkl} e^k_{(0)}\wedge e^l_{(0)}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: f^{ij}_(0) is symmetric
nodes.statement: The matrix $f^{ij}_{(0)}$ is related to the Ricci curvature, see below, and is hence symmetric.

nodes.name: gamma_(2) in terms of f
nodes.statement: From (\ref{X-12}) we get \begin{eqnarray} \gamma_{(2)}^{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \left( f^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} {\rm Tr}(f_{(0)}) \delta^{ij}\right). \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Curvature of the boundary metric from f
nodes.statement: Now, from (\ref{f-ij}) the Riemann curvature of the zeroth order metric is given by \begin{eqnarray} R^{ij \, mn}_{(0)} = \epsilon^{ikj} f^{kl}_{(0)} \epsilon^{lmn}. \end{eqnarray} Hence the Ricci tensor is \begin{eqnarray} R_{(0)\,ij} = R_{(0)\,imj}{}^m = f_{(0)\,ij} - \delta_{ij} {\rm Tr}(f_{(0)}). \end{eqnarray} or equivalently \begin{eqnarray} f^{ij}_{(0)} = R^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{2} \delta^{ij} R_{(0)}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Riemann and Ricci curvature of gamma_(0) in terms of f_(0); equivalently f = Ric - R delta/2.

nodes.name: gamma_(2) via Schouten-type tensor
nodes.statement: Hence, we can equivalently write $\gamma_{(2)}$ as \begin{eqnarray} \gamma_{(2)}^{ij} =\frac{1}{2}\left( R^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} R_{(0)} \delta^{ij}\right). \end{eqnarray}
conclusions: \gamma_{(2)}^{ij} =\frac{1}{2}\left( R^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} R_{(0)} \delta^{ij}\right).

nodes.name: Asymptotic expansion of AH connections solving the field equations
nodes.statement: Thus, the asymptotically hyperbolic connections satisfying field equations take the form \begin{eqnarray} A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}\Big(e_{(0)}^i+\rho \omega_{(0)}^i+\frac{\rho^2}{2} \left( R^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} R_{(0)} \delta^{ij}\right) e_{(0)}^j+\rho^3 e_{(3)}^i+\cdots\Big). \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: the asymptotically hyperbolic connections satisfying field equations
conclusions: A^i=\frac{1}{\rho}\Big(e_{(0)}^i+\rho \omega_{(0)}^i+\frac{\rho^2}{2} \left( R^{ij}_{(0)} - \frac{1}{3} R_{(0)} \delta^{ij}\right) e_{(0)}^j+\rho^3 e_{(3)}^i+\cdots\Big).
nodes.statement_short: Connection analogue of the Fefferman-Graham expansion: A = (e_0 + rho omega_0 + rho^2 Schouten-type term + rho^3 e_3 + ...)/rho.

nodes.name: Gauge equivalence with the metric connection
nodes.statement: This differs from the connection (\ref{A-metric}) computed from an asymptotically hyperbolic metric with the absence of a $d\rho$ term. The two connections are nonetheless gauge equivalent.

nodes.name: Universality of the expansion across deformed theories
nodes.statement: We emphasise that the connection has the expansion as above for any member of our class of gravity theories, including GR.
assumptions: any member of our class of gravity theories, including GR
conclusions: the connection has the expansion as above

nodes.name: Analogy with the metric expansion; free data e_(3)
nodes.statement: This expansion is the analog of the metric expansion reviewed in the Introduction. The freedom that arises in the expansion of $m^{ij}$ at order $m_{(3)}^{ij}$ translates into the freedom in $X_{(3)}^{ij}$, which in turn translates into $e_{(3)}^i$ being not completely determined.

nodes.name: Order-by-order solvability after free data
nodes.statement: After the free part of $e_{(3)}^i$ is specified, the connection equations can be solved order by order in the expansion parameter, with no further ambiguity.
assumptions: the free part of $e_{(3)}^i$ is specified
conclusions: the connection equations can be solved order by order in the expansion parameter, with no further ambiguity

nodes.name: Curvature wedge products of the solution
nodes.statement: It is a useful exercise to compute the matrix $X^{ij}$ of curvature wedge products directly from (\ref{A-final}). We have \begin{multline} F^i\wedge F^j = - 2\frac{d\rho}{\rho^2} \wedge e_{(0)}^{(i} \wedge \frac{1}{2\rho^2} \epsilon^{j)kl} e_{(0)}^k \wedge e_{(0)}^l \\ -2\frac{d\rho}{\rho^2} \wedge e_{(0)}^{(i} \wedge ( f^{j)}_{(0)} + \epsilon^{j)kl} e_{(0)}^k \wedge(Re_{(0)})^l )\\ + 2d\rho \wedge(R e_{(0)})^{(i} \wedge \frac{1}{2\rho^2} \epsilon^{j)kl} e_{(0)}^k \wedge e_{(0)}^l + \ldots, \end{multline} where we denoted \begin{eqnarray} (Re_{(0)})^i:= \left( R^{ij} - \frac{1}{3} R \delta^{ij}\right) e_{(0)}^j, \end{eqnarray} and dots stand for terms of order $d\rho/\rho$ and higher. These terms vanish when the trace is taken, and so will not contribute into our computation of the divergent terms below.

nodes.name: Expansion of M (GR case)
nodes.statement: As we have previously established, this matrix has the following expansion (in the case of GR): \begin{eqnarray} M = \frac{3}{\Lambda} \left( {\mathbb I} + O(\rho^3) \right), \end{eqnarray} where moreover the order $\rho^3$ term is tracefree.

nodes.name: Argument that divergences are those of Tr(F^F)
nodes.statement: We now combine (\ref{X-soln}) and (\ref{M-soln}) to compute the divergent contributions. The leading term in (\ref{X-soln}) is a multiple of the identity matrix. Hence, because of the trace free character of the order $\rho^3$ term in (\ref{M-soln}), there is no contribution from that term and this is why it was not necessary to compute it.
nodes.statement_short: The leading wedge-product matrix is pure trace, so the trace-free rho^3 term of M does not contribute to divergences.

nodes.name: Divergences of the action equal Chern-Simons
nodes.statement: Thus, all the divergent terms in (\ref{action}) are the same as those in the functional \begin{eqnarray} \frac{3}{\Lambda}\int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = - \frac{3}{\Lambda} S^{CS}_{X_\epsilon}[A] , \end{eqnarray} where $S^{CS}$ is the Chern-Simons functional (\ref{CS}).
conclusions: all the divergent terms in (\ref{action}) are the same as those in the functional
nodes.statement_short: All divergences of the bulk action coincide with those of (3/Lambda) Tr(F^F) = -(3/Lambda) S_CS on the cut-off boundary.

nodes.name: Orientation sign
nodes.statement: The minus sign in (\ref{bulk-bound}) is due to our choice of the orientation: we have placed the asymptotic boundary in the bulk integral on the lower limit of integration.

nodes.name: Counter terms combine into the Chern-Simons action
nodes.statement: We thus see that the boundary term necessary to remove the divergences arising in the bulk integration is just a multiple of the boundary Chern-Simons action.
conclusions: the boundary term necessary to remove the divergences arising in the bulk integration is just a multiple of the boundary Chern-Simons action

nodes.name: Chern-Simons term serves two purposes
nodes.statement: This gives another reason for selecting the Chern-Simons functional of the boundary connection as the boundary term in our action principle: it serves both the purpose of making the variational principle well-defined as well as renormalising the action by subtracting the divergent contributions.

nodes.name: Explicit divergences
nodes.statement: Taking the trace of (\ref{X-soln}), and using the fact that the matrix in $(Re_{(0)})$ is trace free, we get \begin{eqnarray} \int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(F\wedge F) = -2 \int_{\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} (3 + \rho^2 {\rm Tr}(f)) + \ldots= -\frac{2}{\epsilon^3} \int_{X_\epsilon} dv_0 - \frac{2}{\epsilon} \int_{X_\epsilon} dv_0 \,{\rm Tr}(f)+ \ldots, \end{eqnarray} where dots stand for finite parts, and $dv_0$ is the volume form for the metric with triad $e_{(0)}$.

nodes.name: Renormalised volume (connection setting)
nodes.statement: Finally, we can define the notion of renormalised volume in the connection setup. We define it as \begin{eqnarray} -2 \Lambda \, RV= \lim_{\epsilon\to 0} \left( \int_\epsilon {\rm Tr}(M F\wedge F) + \frac{3}{\Lambda} S^{CS}_{X_\epsilon} \right), \end{eqnarray} where we took (\ref{volume}) into account.
nodes.definiendum: renormalised volume in the connection setup
nodes.statement_short: -2 Lambda RV is the limit of the cut-off bulk action plus (3/Lambda) times the boundary Chern-Simons functional.

nodes.name: 1/epsilon coefficient differs from metric setup
nodes.statement: We note that the coefficient in front of $1/\epsilon$ term in our connection setup is different from that in the metric setup, see (\ref{RV}). This is because we are working in a different gauge and the metric as computed from the connection would have had the mixed $d\rho dx^i$ terms. These would change the computation of the renormalised volume above. There would be extra sub-leading terms present that would change the coefficient in front of the $1/\epsilon$ term.

nodes.name: Chern-Simons functional under large gauge transformations
nodes.statement: However, as is well-known, Chern--Simons functional is not gauge invariant. It remains invariant under small gauge transformations (homotopic to the identity). Under the so-called large gauge transformations, Chern--Simons functional changes (in our normalisation) by an integral multiple of $8\pi^2$, so that $S^{CS}/4\pi$ changes by a multiple of $2\pi$. More precisely, there is a natural isomorphism $H_3(\rm{SU}(2)) \cong \mathbb{Z}$; now given a gauge transformation $g \colon X \to \rm{SU}(2)$ of the trivial bundle, write $n$ for the integer $g_*[X] \in H_3(\rm{SU}(2)) \cong {\mathbb Z}$, then $S^{CS}(g^*(A)) = 8\pi^2 n + S^{CS}(A)$.
assumptions: given a gauge transformation $g \colon X \to \rm{SU}(2)$ of the trivial bundle, write $n$ for the integer $g_*[X] \in H_3(\rm{SU}(2)) \cong {\mathbb Z}$
nodes.statement_short: CS is invariant under small gauge transformations and shifts by 8 pi^2 n under a large one of degree n.
also_stated_at: As is well-known, the Chern-Simons invariant of an ${\rm SU}(2)$ connection on a compact 3-manifold is not invariant under so-called large gauge transformations.
The Chern-Simons invariant of an ${\rm SO}(3)$ connection is not gauge-invariant, being defined only modulo multiples of $8\pi^2$, see below.

nodes.name: Renormalised volume defined modulo a constant
nodes.statement: Thus, our renormalised volume is defined modulo addition of a constant: \begin{eqnarray} RV\in \mathbb{R}\quad {\rm mod} \quad \frac{3}{2\Lambda^2} 8\pi^2. \end{eqnarray}
conclusions: our renormalised volume is defined modulo addition of a constant:

nodes.name: On-shell Einstein-Hilbert action is a multiple of volume
nodes.statement: The Riemannian signature Einstein--Hilbert action \begin{eqnarray} S_{\rm EH} = -\frac{1}{16\pi G} \int \sqrt{g} (R-2\Lambda) \end{eqnarray} becomes, on Einstein metrics $R_{\mu\nu}=\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$, a multiple of the total volume of the space \begin{eqnarray} S = -\frac{\Lambda}{8\pi G} V. \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: on Einstein metrics $R_{\mu\nu}=\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$
conclusions: a multiple of the total volume of the space

nodes.name: Path integral over connections
nodes.statement: In the connection setup, we want to do a path integral over connections \begin{eqnarray} \int {\cal D}A \, \exp{\frac{i}{\hbar} S[A]}. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Argument for the action ambiguity
nodes.statement: As we have described above, our action in the connection setting is just a multiple of the total volume of the space, and we should clearly use the same multiple as in (\ref{S-EH-on-shell}). Now, as we discussed, in the asymptotically hyperbolic setting we need to add a multiple of the Chern--Simons functional of the boundary connection to our bulk action, to regularise it and to make the variational principle well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: The action is a multiple of the volume plus a Chern-Simons boundary term, which is only defined modulo large gauge shifts.

nodes.name: Connection action defined modulo a constant
nodes.statement: This means that in the asymptotically hyperbolic setting, our connection action is again only defined modulo a constant: \begin{eqnarray} S \in \mathbb{R} \quad {\rm (mod)} \quad \frac{3}{8 G \Lambda} 2\pi. \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: in the asymptotically hyperbolic setting
conclusions: our connection action is again only defined modulo a constant:

nodes.name: Quantisation condition 1/(8 G hbar) = N Lambda/3
nodes.statement: If we want the path integral to be insensitive to this ambiguity we should require that the phase in $\exp{i S/\hbar}$ is an integer multiple of $2\pi$. This gives the following quantisation condition \begin{eqnarray} \frac{1}{8 G \hbar} = \frac{N\Lambda}{3}, \qquad N\in {\mathbb N}. \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: we want the path integral to be insensitive to this ambiguity
conclusions: This gives the following quantisation condition

nodes.name: Hubble length quantised in Planck units
nodes.statement: To put it differently, introducing the Planck length $l_P^2 = G\hbar$ and the Hubble length $\Lambda/3=1/L^2$ we get \begin{eqnarray} L^2 = 8 N l_P^2, \end{eqnarray} the Hubble length is quantised in units of the Planck length.
assumptions: introducing the Planck length $l_P^2 = G\hbar$ and the Hubble length $\Lambda/3=1/L^2$
conclusions: the Hubble length is quantised in units of the Planck length
nodes.statement_short: Requiring a well-defined path integral gives L^2 = 8 N l_P^2: the cosmological constant is quantised.

nodes.name: Extrapolation to positive Lambda
nodes.statement: Of course, we have derived the above quantisation condition working with asymptotically hyperbolic connections corresponding to negative scalar curvature. Observations indicate that our Universe is filled with dark energy whose equation of state is consistent with having a {\it positive} cosmological constant. If we extrapolate (\ref{quant}) to the setting of positive $\Lambda$, then, for all quantities as observed $N$ is very large $8N = L^2/l_P^2 \sim 10^{120}$, and is the number embodying the famous cosmological constant problem.

nodes.name: Cosmological constant quantisation in 3D Chern-Simons gravity
nodes.statement: It should also be said that the quantisation condition (\ref{quant}) is reminiscent of what happens in the setting of Riemannian signature gravity in three dimensions (with positive $\Lambda$), where the full action, not just the boundary term as here, is given by the Chern-Simons functional of a certain ${\rm SU}(2)$-connection. Similar large gauge transformation considerations show that the cosmological constant must be quantised in this setting, see e.g., \cite{Freidel:1998ua} where this fact is reviewed.

nodes.name: Chern-Gauss-Bonnet boundary term renormalises volume (Anderson)
nodes.statement: We also note that the fact that the Chern--Simons functional renormalises the volume is analogous to the statement in \cite{Anderson} that the boundary term at infinity in the Chern--Gauss--Bonnet formula renormalises the volume.

nodes.name: Admissibility of the gauge (Appendix A)
nodes.statement: In this Appendix we show how the gauge freedom of diffeomorphisms plus gauge transformations can be used to simplify the connection asymptotic expansion problem. Under an infinitesimal diffeomorphism generated by $\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho\in\Gamma(T\overline{M})$ and infinitesimal gauge transformation generated by $\varphi^i\in C^\infty(\overline{M},\mathfrak {su}(2))$ the connection (\ref{as-hyperb-conn}) transformations as \begin{multline*} \delta_{\xi+\rho\lambda\partial_\rho+\varphi}A^i =\frac{1}{\rho}({\mathcal L}^X_\xi e^i_{(0)}+\epsilon^{ijk}e^j_{(0)}\varphi^k-\lambda e^i_{(0)}) \\ +{\mathcal L}^X_\xi \omega^i_{(0)}+d^X\varphi^i+\epsilon^{ijk}\omega_{(0)}^j\varphi^k+{\mathcal L}^X_\xi a^i+\epsilon^{ijk}a^j\varphi^k+\rho(\lambda \dot a^i+b^id^X\lambda) \\ +\Big(\frac{1}{\rho}\iota_{\dot \xi}e^i_{(0)}+\iota_{\dot \xi}\omega^i_{(0)}+\dot \varphi^i+\iota_{\dot \xi}a^i+\iota_\xi d^X b^i+\epsilon^{ijk} b^j\varphi^k+\lambda b^i+\rho(\lambda\dot b^i+\dot \lambda b^i)\Big)d\rho \end{multline*} The idea now is to set $b^i$ and the anti-symmetric and trace parts of (the subleading orders of) $\langle a^i,e^j_{(0)}\rangle$ to zero by (infinitesimal) diffeomorphisms and gauge transformations. nodes.name: Hamiltonian derivation of the 3+1 field equations
nodes.statement: We here show how to derive the 3+1 decomposition of the field equations described in \ref{subsec: Init val form} from a Hamiltonian formulation. As before, we decompose the connection $A^i$ as $$A^i=\alpha^i+\beta^id\rho,$$ and its curvature as $$F_A^i=f_\alpha^i-(\dot\alpha^i-d^X_\alpha\beta^i)\wedge d\rho,$$ where $d^X_\alpha$ is the covariant exterior derivative with respect to connection $\alpha^i$ along the hypersurface $\rho=\text{const}$, and $f^i_\alpha$ is the curvature of $\alpha^i$. The matrix $X^{ij}$, defined up to scale, now reads \[ X^{ij} {\mathcal V}= F^i \wedge F^j = f_\alpha^{(i}\wedge (\dot\alpha^{j)}-d^X_\alpha\beta^{j)})\wedge d\rho. \] The Lagrangian \eqref{action} thus take the following 3+1 form \begin{eqnarray} S[A,M,\mu] = \int_M \left( M^{ij} f_\alpha^{i} \wedge \left( \dot\alpha^{j}-d^X_\alpha\beta^{j}\right) - \mu \, g(M) \right) \wedge d\rho. \end{eqnarray} where we implemented the constraint with a 3-form Lagrange multiplier $\mu \in \Lambda^3\left(X \right)$.\\ The associated momenta are: \begin{align*} \pi^i := \pi^i_{\alpha} = M^{ij} f^i_\alpha \;; & & \pi^i_{\beta}=0 \;; & & \pi^{ij}_M =0 \;; & & \pi_{\mu}=0. \end{align*} Note that $\dot{\alpha}$ do not appear in the right-hand-side of the first equation, thus we cannot invert the system and write $\pi_{\alpha}$ as a function of $\dot{\alpha}$. The same is true for all other momenta. This means that we have to keep track of the above equations as constraints on the phase space. The generalised Hamiltonian associated to the Lagrangian has all these constraints added with corresponding Lagrange multipliers \begin{multline} H[\alpha, \pi, \beta, \pi_{\beta}, M , \pi_M ,u,v,w] = \int_X -\beta^{i}\left( d^X_\alpha\pi^i \right) + \mu \, g(M) \\ + u^i \wedge \left(\pi^i- M^{ij} f^j_\alpha\right) + v^i \wedge \pi^i_{\beta} + w^{ij} \wedge \pi^{ij}_M + x \pi_{\mu} \end{multline} where $u$, $v$, $w$ and $x$ are Lagrange multipliers introduced to take care of the constraints on the momenta. We also used integration by parts to make explicit the role of $\beta^i$ as a Lagrange multiplier. We have the secondary constraints: \begin{align*} \dot{\pi}_{\beta}=0& \Leftrightarrow d^X_{\alpha} \pi^i =0 \\ \dot{\pi}_{M} =0& \Leftrightarrow \mu \frac{\partial g}{\partial M^{ij}} = u^{(i} \wedge f^{j)}_{\alpha} \\ \dot{\pi}_{\mu}=0& \Leftrightarrow g\left(M \right)=0 \end{align*} At this point, Hamilton's equations read: \begin{align*} &\dot{\pi}^i = -[\beta,\pi]^i + d^X_{\alpha} \left( M^{ij} u^j\right) \;;& & \dot{\alpha}^i = d^X_{\alpha} \beta^i + u^i. \end{align*} We can now solve for $u^i$ and obtain the first equation in (\ref{feqs}). The second secondary constraint becomes \begin{align} \mu \frac{\partial g}{\partial M^{ij}} = X^{ij} \end{align} Altogether, we have reproduced the complete equations of the theory from the Hamiltonian viewpoint. In principle, we should also take care of the secondary constraint $\left\{ H , \pi^i- M^{ij} f^j_\alpha \right\}=0$ together with tertiary constraints possibly arising. We do not carry out this analysis here as it is not necessary to obtain the field equations. We also note that one way to complete the Hamiltonian analysis is via an Ashtekar-like Hamiltonian formulation, which for modified theories considered here was described in \cite{Krasnov:2008zz}.
